reviewer.name: Claude Sonnet, fresh subagent (cold reader 2)
reviewer.origin: Claude Agent tool subagent, model sonnet, a fresh context with only this brief and its files, launched 2026-10-26 by session_01Mxpoi6tFT3FgKmBvtGjRtS (the writer's session)

evidence: Judged the draft “When you're done, make sure to come back the other way.” against SOURCE.txt (replaced words “And when you're done, come back the other way.”; meaning to keep, from his published guide: “reverse the journey when you finish”) and in its CONTEXT paragraph. Change check: the_change says Emulate's sentence from sample cm replaces the source sentence. DRAFT.txt is exactly that sentence; it appears once in CONTEXT.txt, in the old sentence's place (after “If you're going to count, do it in a way that makes sense in your world.” and before “(You can borrow qualities, but don't change who you are.)”), and the replaced words no longer appear. No AI-writer fix is claimed and none is needed. Meaning: “come back the other way” is the same step as “reverse the journey when you finish”. The only differences are the dropped “And” and the added “make sure to”, which stresses the same instruction and adds no new step, condition, fact or safety rule, so no claim is added. Seam and voice: the paragraph is plain, casual directives (“Keep it simple”, “just do one”, “try to keep them related”, “whatever”), and “make sure to” sits in that register; I felt no seam and no different writer. The straight apostrophe in “you're” matches the rest of that paragraph (in the body, curly ones appear only in the next paragraph's last two sentences). “the other way” has the same anchor as in the old sentence (“one way of coming back” in the section's first paragraph), so it is no less clear than before. Dropping “And” loses one spoken connective, but the section keeps the habit (“And then read it out loud” in the next paragraph) and the neighbouring sentences here also open without a conjunction. Tell rows: I went through T01 to T29 and C01 to C04 on the draft in its context and found none actually happening. Looked at hardest: T02 (the paragraph is a short run of conditional rules, but that is the existing paragraph's structure; the swap is one sentence, same job, same place, adds no rule, and the paragraph is uneven and carries asides, the “whatever” list and the closing parenthetical, so it is not an engineered manual cadence); T22 (a plain instruction, no reassurance or anticipated feeling, and the paragraph has stance around it); T07, T10, T11, T19 (not filler, a permission formula, a bridge or an announcement); T15 (“make sure to” is a common phrase, not a rarer word swapped in); T20, T28, T29 (not the paragraph's last sentence, the parenthetical follows it; no summary or uplift); T26 (“come back” echoes “one way of coming back” as a callback to the same step, which is a real job); T13 and T09 (the swap adds and removes no aside, reason or callback, and the sentence is short among sentences of very different lengths); C02 (no pronoun but “you”); C03 and C04 (no first-person fact, no study, person or product). One note on the writer's ledger: its T14 and T15 lines say the draft puts back a point Emulate dropped; here the draft is Emulate's sentence unchanged, so that wording does not apply, but it changes no judgment. Linter, D9 “follows the source order”: accepted. This is a one-sentence swap in its own place, so the paragraph's order is the old order by construction and 1/1 agreement says nothing about the draft; the T13 and T09 checks it asks for came out absent as above. Linter, E36/E41 “heavy second person”: accepted. 9.1 per 100 is one “you're” in an 11-word sentence (the replaced sentence also had one “you're”, in 9 words); the guide addresses the reader as “you” throughout and “when you're done” has no natural second-person-free form here, so the figure reflects the sentence's size, not a coach-register pattern.
